fixes.explanation: Eighteen it is, friend. Luke says she had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years, hunched over and unable to stand up straight (Luke 13:11). That's a long, long time to carry that. I think eighteen years is worth slowing down for.

Twelve is close, but it's not this woman's number. Luke says she had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years (Luke 13:11). That's six more years than twelve, and she was hunched over and unable to stand straight through all of them. I think eighteen is worth remembering.

Thirty-eight is a big number, but it's not this woman's number. Luke says she had been disabled for eighteen years (Luke 13:11). Eighteen years of being hunched over and unable to stand straight is already a long time. Eighteen is the number the text gives.

Right on the money. Luke says, "When Jesus saw her, He called her over…" (Luke 13:12). He saw her, and He called her over. No waiting, no committee meeting. I think being noticed like that meant a lot.

Not a night's wait, friend. The text says that after He placed His hands on her, "…immediately she straightened up…" (Luke 13:13). It didn't take until the next morning. It happened right then, in the synagogue.

Good guess, but the text gives a different reason. Luke says the leader "…was indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath." (Luke 13:14). The touch is not given as the reason for his indignation. The healing on the Sabbath is what bothered him.

False is right. The leader "…told the crowd." "There are six days for work… So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath." (Luke 13:14). He spoke to the crowd, not to Jesus. The text doesn't say why he chose to speak to them.

Exactly. Jesus asks, "Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water?" (Luke 13:15). The ox or donkey gets untied and led to water on the Sabbath. I think Jesus was making His point with something they already did.

Humiliated is right. Luke says, "…all His adversaries were humiliated." (Luke 13:17). That's what the text says happened to them after Jesus spoke. It's the opposite of what happened to the crowd, who rejoiced.
Rejoices, yes. Luke says, "…the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things He was doing." (Luke 13:17). The whole crowd, not just a few. They rejoiced at all the glorious things Jesus was doing.
Encouraged sounds friendly, but it's not the word. Luke says His adversaries "were humiliated." (Luke 13:17). Humiliated is what the text says. Encouraged is a good guess, but it isn't in the verse.
